source.title: Return to Play, Performance, and Career Longevity After Shoulder Labral Repair in the National Football League: A Matched Cohort Analysis

paper.citation: Dillon MR, Mastroianni MA, Frappa N, Evoniuk C, Curtis W, Trofa DP, Jobin CM, Ablove R, Levine WN, Ahmad CS. Return to Play, Performance, and Career Longevity After Shoulder Labral Repair in the National Football League: A Matched Cohort Analysis. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2026;14(7):23259671261454331. doi:10.1177/23259671261454331.
paper.abstract: This retrospective matched-cohort study used public injury reporting and NFL participation and performance data to examine return to play, workload, PFF grade, and career longevity after reported isolated shoulder labral repair. Cases were matched with controls by season, position, age, and preindex snap rate.
paper.tldr: Most identified NFL players returned after reported shoulder labral repair, and first-season participation workload was broadly similar to matched controls. Defensive-player performance grades declined more than controls, but public-record limitations and selection of established returners prevent clinical or causal interpretation.
paper.methods: The authors identified procedures through injury transactions, team or NFL communications, and corroborating media reports. Return was the first regular-season snap after the reported surgery date. Cases and controls were matched by season and position, then age and preindex snap rate. Outcomes included games, snaps, snaps per game, season-level PFF grades, and postreturn career duration.
paper.findings: Ninety-six of 111 identified episodes returned to NFL play, an 86.5% rate, at a median 265 days; 73.9% returned within one year and 84.7% within two years. First-season changes in games and snap workload did not differ significantly from controls. Defensive cases had larger PFF-grade declines than controls, while offensive-grade differences and career-duration comparisons were not statistically significant.
paper.limitations: Public reporting could not confirm diagnosis, tear characteristics, bone loss, operative details, rehabilitation, recurrence, or clinical milestones. Requiring at least 100 snaps before and after return selected healthier, established returners for performance analysis. PFF grades are influenced by scheme, coaching, role, utilization, concurrent injury, and other unmeasured factors. The observational design cannot establish that surgery caused any outcome.
paper.practicalImplications: Separate participation, workload tolerance, role-specific performance, and career continuity when discussing return after shoulder labral repair. Use the reported timeline as descriptive NFL context, not as an individual prognosis or clearance target.
paper.athleteDev: Rebuild contact tolerance, position-specific shoulder demands, football workload, and technical performance progressively. Evaluate the athlete's actual role and preinjury baseline rather than treating a return to snaps as full performance restoration.
paper.rtp: This study provides descriptive return timing and postreturn outcomes but no clinical clearance criteria. Individual decisions still require tissue and symptom status, strength and function, contact exposure, position demands, recurrence risk, athlete preference, and interdisciplinary judgment.
